webTitle: Nasdaq hits record high after weaker-than-expected US jobs report – as it happened

fields.headline: Nasdaq hits record high after weaker-than-expected US jobs report – as it happened
fields.trailText: US economy only added 29,000 jobs in September, which might deter the Federal Reserve from raising interest rates
fields.bodyText: Time to wrap up…. US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. More here: The weak jobs report cut the chances of the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates this month, helping to push down US government bond yields and sending the Nasdaq stock index to a record high. In other news… G7 countries have agreed to release 100mn barrels of diesel and crude oil from their strategic reserves, following pressure from the White House. The move came as the average price of diesel in the UK climbed to a record £2 a litre….. ….and the government insisted that the UK is not facing a diesel shortage. Soaring energy costs pushed inflation in the eurozone up to a three-year high of 3.8% last month. Food inflation pressure is also rising, after prices hit their highest level in almost four years. After a choppy week, the UK stock market has closed with a small daily gain. The FTSE 100 index has ended the session up 33.7 points or 0.3% at 10,461 points. Mining stocks were among today’s risers. But for the week, that still leaves the Footsie down 2.18%, its biggest weekly drop since mid-April. The odds of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates at its next meeting later this month have dropped today. According to CME Fedwatch, an October rate hike is now only a 20.5% chance. That’s down from 24.4% yesterday, and 64% a week ago when the markets were much more confident the Fed would tighten policy. In another boost to the financial markets, the G7 have agreed to release as much as 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks. The move follows pressure from the Trump administration to quell rising fuel prices. If it works, then it will remove some of the inflationary pressure that has pushed up bond yields this week (before today’s recovery). Emmanuel Macron, France’s president, says the release will take place over the next four months. It is being coordinated by the International Energy Agency. A statement released by Macron’s office, says: “We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over 4 months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners.” Our Europe Live blog has more details: Newsflash: America’s technology stock index has hit a record high, as traders express relief that today’s jobs report might dampen the pressure to raise US interest rates. The Nasdaq Composite has jumped by 1.6% in early trading in New York. Rocket Lab (+7.4%) are leading the risers, followed by UK-based chip designer ARM Holdings (+6.9%). Stocks are up more broadly, with the S&P 500 index rising by 1%. Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, explains why the slowdown in hiring across the US economy last month has cheered investors: ‘’There’s been a ripple of relief on financial markets as hopes rise that the Fed won’t have to go so hard and fast in raising interest rates. Treasury and gilt yields have eased off, and equity markets are on a rising tide, as the rush of worry has started to recede. The latest US jobs figures came in weaker than expected, with just 29,000 jobs added in September, compared with forecasts of around 90,000. That’s a marked slowdown, although some of the weakness reflects a fall in government payrolls. But pay packets indicate that employees don’t have the upper hand in demanding higher wages, with hourly earnings rising by just 0.1% over the month, taking annual wage growth down to 3%, its lowest rate since the pandemic. The figures suggest the jobs engine is losing a little steam, but isn’t spluttering to a halt, so the snapshot has been greeted as a dose of better news and a sign that the Fed may be a tad more wary about hiking borrowing costs. Here's Nancy Vanden Houten, Lead US Economist at Oxford Economics, on today’s nonfarm payrolls data release: The softer than expected September employment report makes a rate hike at the October meeting a closer call. However, we think the upside risks to inflation are still a bigger concern for the Federal Reserve and expect they will raise rates at the end of the month. Nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000 in September and there were downward revisions to job gains for July and August. Still, on a trend basis, job growth is well in line with our estimate of the breakeven pace of job growth. The unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% in September as the prime-age labor force participation rate continues to recover some of the plunge that occurred in June. Looking ahead, we expect the unemployment rate to hold steady around 4.2% with the risk skewed to the downside as labor force growth continues to slow. An October hike in US interest rates is now “firmly on the back foot”, predicts Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management: “A softer-than-expected jobs report should put an October Fed hike firmly on the back foot. Weaker payrolls, softer wage growth and a higher unemployment rate all point to a labour market that’s cooling rather than reaccelerating. That should take some steam out of Treasury yields and reduce the urgency for the Fed to act. CPI remains the decisive release, but today’s data argues for patience, not panic. The Fed needs to see a reacceleration in inflation, not just resilience in growth, to justify another hike this year.” Here’s Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, on today’s jobs report: The softer employment gain and tick up in the unemployment rate in September is not enough to spoil the image of a labour market which is broadly performing well, though it may help to trim investors’ expectations for how far the Fed will eventually tighten back towards our view for two more rate hikes. The 29,000 rise in non-farm payrolls in September was notably weaker than the consensus 90,000 estimate, but not disastrous. A 17,000 drag in government payrolls was partly to blame. Meanwhile, the softer 23,000 rise in healthcare & social assistance payrolls rose may be linked to the Trump administration’s recent decision to rescind Temporary Protected Status (TPS) and working authorisation for 350,000 migrants. US workers’ average earnings growth has also slowed, which is not good news for Donald Trump ahead of next month’s midterm elections. Today’s jobs repot shows that in September, average hourly earnings were 3.0% higher than a year ago, down from 3.1% in August. Nic Puckrin, a former Goldman Sachs analyst, explains: “Today’s ice-cold report shows the jobs market may not be as healthy as previous data might have suggested. Wage growth is more anaemic than expected at 3%, while payrolls came in well below expectations at 28,000, with August also revised down. This is a fly in the ointment for the Fed: it’s forcing the central bank to choose between two evils. Hike again, and you risk tipping the scale on unemployment at a time when Americans are already struggling with the cost-of-living crisis. Hold, and inflation could get out of control. The US dollar is edging lower against some other major currencies. It’s down by 0.5% against the Japanese yen, to ¥157.23/$. It’s also lost 0.15% against the pound, which has risen to $1.322. The dollar index, which tracks the greenback against a basket of other currencies, is down 0.25%. Wall Street is set to rally when trading begins in 45 minutes, as today’s weak jobs report cools some fears of future interest rate rises. The Dow Jones industrial average is forecast to rise by 0.85%, according to futures market pricing, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 up 1% in pre-market trading. Today’s weak US jobs report is bringing some comfort to the bond markets! The prices of US Treasuries are rising, which is pulling down the yield (or rate of return) on these bonds away from the multi-year highs set earlier this week. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries has fallen by 6 basis points (or 0.06 of a percentage point) to 5.174%. That pulls it away from the 24-year high recorded yesterday. 30-year US Treasury bonds are recovering too; the yield here is down by 4.5bps to 5.568%. That’s not because bond investors like the sound of Americans strugging to find work. It’s because it will be harder for the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, to fight inflation, if the jobs market is weakening. The Fed has a dual mandate – to deliver price stability and full employment. Health care continued to be a creator of jobs last month – hiring increased by 17,000 in September, including gains at ambulatory health care services and in hospitals. Employment in construction rose by 11,000 Manufacturing employment rose by 9,000. But financial activities fell by 7,000. The BLS adds: Employment also showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; wholesale trade; retail trade; transportation and warehousing; information; professional and business services; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. Newsflash: the US economy added much fewer jobs than expected last month, after a sharp slowdown in hiring. Nonfarm payroll employment rose by just 29,000 last month, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported. That’s much weaker than the 90,000 new jobs which economists had expected. The BLS says: Employment in all major industries changed little over the month. In another blow, August’s jobs report has been revised down to show that 29,000 fewer jobs were created than first estimated – 133,000, not 162,000. And July’s jobs gains have been revised down by 31,000, from +21,000 to -10,000, meaning the US economy lost jobs in July. French president Emmanuel Macron ⁠will chair a video call with his ⁠counterparts from ⁠the G7 from 2.30pm local time (1.30pm BST) to discuss possible measures on the world markets ⁠for crude and refined products, the ‌Elysee Palace ‌has said in a statement. This follow US pressure on European nations to release additional diesel stockpiles in an attempt to reduce surging fuel prices. UK mortgage rates have hit the highest levels in more than two years this morning, pushed up by the turmoil in the bond markets. The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate has now risen to 5.96%, up from 5.93% yesterday, Moneyfacts reports. That’s the highest since 30 June 2024. The average 5-year fixed residential mortgage rate has risen to 5.98%, up from 5.95% yesterday, and the highest since 29 September 2023. This morning’s jump in eurozone inflation hasn’t prevented stock markets in the region recovering some of yesterday’s losses. Germany’s DAX index has gained 1.1% so far today, while France’s CAC is up 0.8%. Traders will be reassured by the drop in the oil price today – Brent crude is still down around 2.4% at $99.87 a barrel. High fuel prices are likely to push eurozone inflation to 4% by the end of the year, predict analysts Bill Diviney and Adrian Quinn at ABN Amro. They told clients: We expect inflation to continue to move higher over the coming months, although the biggest of the rises is probably behind us with today’s release. Our base case assumes energy prices stay elevated well into 2027, and the broadening pass-through from energy to other categories is expected to push inflation to a peak of a little over 4% by the turn of the year. The still-rising inflation trajectory alongside the continued diplomatic failure to fully resolve the energy supply crunch is likely to keep the ECB’s Governing Council hiking rates over the coming months. We expect two additional rate hikes by the ECB, ultimately taking the deposit rate to 3%. The UK government moved to avert panic at the pumps early this morning by insisting that Britain is not facing a diesel shortage, after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel. The transport minister Keir Mather said on Friday that the UK has a wide range of sources of the fuel and is in talks with other European countries over the potential release of emergency diesel stockpiles. “I want to reassure people that they can still go to the pump and fill up with diesel because the supply we have to the UK is inherently resilient,” he said, speaking on ITV’s Good Morning Britain. “The flows of diesel into the UK come from a variety of sources, and that is resilient.” The wholesale price of diesel in Europe has fallen sharply today, the Financial Times, reports, as European countries come under pressure from the Trump administration to release their motor fuel stocks. The FT has spotted that the continent’s benchmark diesel futures contract fell by nearly 6% to as low as $1364 a tonne, the equivalent of around $185 a barrel. Yesterday, UK government ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission (EC), Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves, amid threats that the US could introduce a ban on diesel exports otherwise. Today’s fresh diesel high was recorded after record fuel prices across Europe in recent weeks, which have ignited calls for political leaders to take action to protect consumers against rising cost pressures. Inflation in the cost of road fuels has outpaced the surge in global oil markets due to a sharp drop in output from refineries damaged by war in the Middle East and in Russia. Before the Ukraine war, Russia provided between 10% and 15% of the world’s diesel supplies. Another 10% of global diesel supplies transited through the strait of Hormuz from Gulf nations before Iran responded to the US-Israeli attacks by disrupting the strait. More here: Petrol prices have risen again too. The average price of a litre of unleaded has risen to 174.71p a litre, which is around 42p more than at the start of the Iran war. Newsflash: The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK has hit £2 for the first time. New data from the RAC shows that diesel hit an average price of 200.01p a litre this morning. That means diesel prices have surged by 40.5% since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, when diesel cost 142.38p a litre. A 55-litre tank of diesel now costs £110.01 – £31.70 more than 28 February, the RAC says. RAC head of policy Simon Williams says: “This is a pump price threshold that no-one wanted to cross – the average price of a litre of diesel has risen to a record 200.01p and is showing no signs of slowing, heaping more misery onto motorists. The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, almost £32 more than it was at the start of the US/Iran war. This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders. In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets. “For an average 45mpg diesel car, the cost works out at an extraordinary 20p per mile, so a driver covering 10,000 miles a year is now spending £2,020 on fuel a year. Households will be tightening the purse strings, while businesses may have no option but to pass these additional costs onto customers. The previous highest price of 199.09p seen in June 2022 is already becoming a distant memory as the conflict in the Middle East continues with no sign of a deal to reopen the critical oil and gas shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Additionally, US threats of a diesel export ban could cause prices to rise even further. Once again, it’s ordinary people who are left footing the bill for events far away, as the UK remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels and imported diesel. Oil is continuing to drop, which would help to ease inflation pressures if this trend continues. Crude is weakening following reports that exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war. Brent crude is now down 2.7% to $99.54 a barrel. Today’s jump in eurozone inflation from 3.2% to 3.8% marks the fastest jump since March, the first month of the Middle East war, reports ING economist Bert Colijn. Colijn told clients: Ouch. Eurozone inflation blew past expectations in September, soaring to its highest level since 2023. Energy inflation remained the main driver of the higher rate. Despite oil prices remaining somewhat below peaks seen in 2022 and this spring, Euro 95 petrol prices have now reached an all-time high. This is weighing significantly on the inflation basket for the moment. At 3.8%, eurozone inflation is the highest since September 2023. Lale Akoner, global market strategist at investment platform eToro, argues that the European Central Bank doesn’t need to react immediately to this morning’s jump in inflation: “Euro-area inflation at 3.8% makes ECB tightening more likely, but the composition of the increase matters. Much of the acceleration is being driven by energy, while core inflation matched expectations at 2.5%. That gives the ECB some room to wait rather than react immediately, particularly as higher bond yields are already tightening financial conditions and weakening demand. The key risk is that the energy shock spreads into wages, services prices and corporate pricing. Services inflation rising to 3.2%, alongside higher consumer inflation expectations, means policymakers cannot assume the shock will fade. The ECB is therefore likely to retain a hawkish bias, even if an October hike remains uncertain. For markets, this is an uncomfortable mix: higher inflation, weaker growth and less scope for rate cuts. It supports the euro, keeps pressure on government bonds and favours companies with pricing power and resilient balance sheets over rate-sensitive sectors and weaker consumers.” Core inflation in the eurozone also inched up last month. Inflation, excluding energy, food, alcohol & tobacco, rose to 2.5% in September up from 2.4% in August. Newsflash: Inflation across the eurozone has surged to almost double the European Central Bank’s 2% target. The euro area inflation rate is expected to be 3.8% in September, statistics body Eurostat has reported, up from 3.2% in August 2026. Energy prices were the biggest driver of inflation across the eurozone – prices were 18.8% higher than in September 2025. That’s an acceleration on August, when energy prices were 14.3% higher year-on-year. Services inflation rose to 3.2%, up from 3.0% in August. Food, alcohol & tobacco inflation inceased to 1.4%, up from 1.1%. But industrial goods inflation slipped to 1.1%, down from 1.2% in August). This jump in inflation could put more pressure on the European Central Bank to raise interest rates (even though that wouldn’t fix the causes of the energy prices shock), to prevent ‘second round effects’, where prices push up wages. Newsflash: World food prices rose in September to their highest in nearly four years as farmers were hit by hot weather and logistics disruptions. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization’s Food Price Index, which tracks a basket of food commodities, has jumped to its highest level since November 2022. The index rose to averaged 136.0 points this month, up from 134.0 for August, with the prices of sugar, meat, oil, dairy and cereals all rising during the month. The report, which gives a great insight into the global food market, reports: The Sugar Price Index surged by 11.9% in August, to its highest level since June 2025. This was riven by fears of weak global sugar supply outlook in the 2026/27 season, partly due to El Niño fears. The FAO says: Persistent hot and dry weather led to a downward revision of sugarbeet yield forecasts in the European Union, where planted area was already anticipated to decline from the previous season, while El Niño-related weather conditions continued to affect production prospects in key producing countries in Asia. Lower sugar production in Brazil’s key Center-South growing region also contributed to the tighter supply outlook. Additionally, India’s announcement of duty-free raw sugar imports further contributed to the increase in international sugar prices. The Cereal Price Index rose by 2.2% in August, to its highest level since May 2024 due to “robust demand, weather-related concerns over crop prospects in key producing regions, and continued uncertainty surrounding Black Sea export flows.” Wheat prices were pushed up by persistent disruptions to Black Sea export logistics, and lower production prospects in parts of Europe following hot and dry weather. [Reminder, the UK is thought to have suffered its worst harvest since detailed records began in 1984]. The Vegetable Oil Price Index rose by 0.6%, its third consecutive monthly increase, to the highest level since June 2022. Higher world palm and soy oil prices, more than offset lower quotations for sunflower and rapeseed oils, with palm oil prices pushed up, in part, by concerns over the potential impact of El Niño-related weather conditions. The Meat Price Index rose 1% in August, due to higher poultry, pig and ovine meat prices. The FAO says: International poultry meat prices rose, reflecting a rebound in Brazilian export prices amid strong global import demand. Pig meat quotations also surged, principally driven by higher prices in the European Union, where high temperatures continued to slow animal growth, limiting the availability of slaughter-ready pigs. And….The Dairy Price Index jumped by 2.3% in August, driven by higher milk powder and cheese prices. French 10-year bond yields are very slightly lower this morning, at 4.925%. Yesterday they rose as high as 4.96%, the highest level since July 2002. The global bond market appears to be steadying this morning. UK government bond prices are recovering some of their recent losses, which is pulling down borrowing costs (yields). The yield on two-year UK bonds has dropped by over six basis points (0.06 of a percentage point) to 4.767% – that could help ease the pressure on mortgage rates. Benchmark 10-year UK bond yields are down 5.5bps to 5.369%, away from the 19-year highs set earlier this week. 30-year bond yields, which hit their highest level since 1998 yesterday, are down too – dropping by 5bps to 5.92%. Bond yields are dropping in sync with the Brent crude oil price, which is down 1% today to $101.19 a barrel. Fears that sharply high oil prices will keep pushing up inflation, forcing central banks to raise interest rates, have been a prime factor behind the bond sell-off. Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, argues that the bond market sell-off presents good opportunities for investors, including in France: “We remain Attractive on fixed income and see the rise in European yields as creating selective opportunities in high-quality bonds. Our core preference remains for short- to medium-term maturities. Within France, we see attractive risk-reward in select agency, covered, and corporate bonds. We also favor stronger investment grade issuers across medium maturities, while higher-risk credit should remain relatively short-dated.” The jump in UK borrowing costs in recent weeks to the highest level in many years has eaten into the ‘fiscal buffer’ which the government created to keep within its fiscal rules. That buffer was £23.6bn back in March, but some economists estimate it could have halved – even before you account for new spending pledges. This means John Healey could face a choice between reporting a smaller buffer (which increases the risk of breaking the fiscal rules), or lifting taxes to boost revenues. Economist Lord O’Neill argues that Healey should accept the buffer will have to be smaller, pointing out that we are facing “remarkable circumstances”. Jim O’Neill told Radio 4’s Today Programme that this might be the wisest thing to do, given the huge unpredictability surrounding Donald Trump and the Iran war. The situation could be very different by the budget, or a few weeks later, and oil prices might have dropped, he argues. As Lord O’Neill puts it: Rather than risking some tax increases in the way previous governments have to just magically hit some number and keep the buffer bigger, in this instance I personally suspect it might be the wisest thing to do. He also argues that the UK economic situation is somewhat better than some people realise, pointing out that the economy grew at an annual rate of 2% in the first half of this year. The euro is trading close to the 17-month low hit yesterday, when the single currency fell by over 0.75% to as low as €1.1214. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, says jitters about France are hurting the euro: The sharp weakening of appetite for French debt is a big issue for the broader euro area and the euro itself. France is the euro area’s second-largest economy — we used to call it the ‘core’, along with Germany, back during the 2012 sovereign debt crisis! So, if concerns spread, other heavily indebted members could also face higher borrowing costs, tightening financial conditions across the region. For the euro, that means weaker growth prospects and a growing risk premium. The EURUSD tanked to 1.1215 yesterday, as the market’s focus shifted from the central-bank convergence/divergence story towards the euro area sovereign debt story. France’s government did try to cool the situation yesterday, by proposing a budget for next year including €43bn in cuts and tax rises. Under the proposed plan, the tax burden would rise while spending growth would be slowed through slashing state spending, and capping increases to pensions and civil servant salaries. Finance minister Roland Lescure explained it was important to put France back on track for deficit reduction. But even with this plan, the French budget deficit would only fall to 5% of GDP next year. Analysts at ING warn that this deficit would be “far too high” to prevent France’s national debt (already 119% of GDP) from rising higher. In a note titled France’s budget offers no quick relief for bond markets, ING say: France’s fiscal package would prevent the deficit from reaching 6.5% of GDP next year, but it would not stabilise public debt. With a difficult political process ahead, French bonds are likely to remain under pressure, while the threshold for ECB intervention remains high Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. Turmoil in the government bond market is reviving memories of the eurozone debt crisis 15 years ago – but this time France is in the firing line. Concerns over Paris’s fiscal position are pushing its borrowing costs up, amid a global sell-off of sovereign debt. This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, a key measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012. Yesterday, the yield on French 10-year government bonds (or OATs) yields jumped to their highest level since 2002, before dipping back as the bond rout eased. Investors are reluctant to eat their OATs due to political uncertainty, with presidential elections scheduled for 2027, and concerns over France’s public debt which has climbed to a record high. Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank strategist, points out that yesterday the Franco-German 10 year spread (+13.9bps) saw its biggest daily jump since March 2020 at the height of the Covid turmoil. Reid told clients this morning: Markets stumbled yesterday as we began Q4, with mounting signs of financial stress focused on Europe. In fact, the daily moves were reminiscent of the Euro crisis in many respects, with sovereign contagion a big talking point. Inflation fears are also pushing up bond yields – and at 10am we get the first reading on how fast prices rose across the eurozone in September. If that doesn’t rock the market, then the latest US jobs report might, as pressure mounts on the US Federal Reserve to consider raising interest rates. The agenda 9am BST: UN’s FAO Food Price Index 10am BST: Eurozone flash inflation reading for September 1.30pm BST: US non-farm payrolls employment report 3pm BST: US factory orders report for August

webTitle: Seth Meyers on Trump: ‘Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for?’

fields.headline: Seth Meyers on Trump: ‘Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for?’
fields.trailText: Late-night hosts talked Trump’s use of taxpayer money to fund campaign ads as GOP candidates distance themselves
fields.bodyText: Late-night hosts dug into Donald Trump’s unpopularity with GOP midterm candidates and his insistence on having US taxpayers foot the bill for recycled campaign ads. Seth Meyers On Thursday’s Late Night, Seth Meyers noted dissent within the Republican party over Donald Trump’s hugely unpopular war with Iran. In the run-up to the midterms next month, several GOP candidates, including Ken Paxton in Texas and Ashley Hinson in Iowa, have run ads calling the war a mistake, though not directly calling out Trump himself. “I’m sorry, you both supported the war, and now you want it to end? Who is that campaign ad for – you?” Meyers asked. “Also by the way, very cool and not at all cowardly to call for an end to the war while not naming the president who started it,” he continued. “But I get it, you guys are in a tough spot. Trump doesn’t care about anyone but himself. When it comes to Republicans running in competitive races, Trump is thinking ‘maybe I help them,’ or” to quote Trump speaking in the Oval Office this week about Iran, “maybe I blow them up.” Trump had previously endorsed Paxton, but “his endorsement came with some very strange and unusual caveats,” said Meyers. As Trump put it in one of many similar asides on Paxton: “He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” “How would you like to have Trump as your wingman?” Meyers laughed. “‘Excuse me, miss, my friend over there thinks you’re very attractive. He, on the other hand, is not attractive at all.’” Later in the segment, Meyers noted: “Trump’s own lackeys are slamming him, his poll numbers are bad, his TV ratings are worse, which is why he’s found a new and totally legal way to get his message out: just air campaign ads on national television using your taxpayer money.” New ads in support of the midterms aired this week that look suspiciously like Trump’s ads from 2024 yet paid for by the US government, raising concerns from Congress. “They literally took a campaign ad they used in 2024 and re-aired it on TV using taxpayer dollars,” Meyers fumed. “He’s $2bn richer than he was two years ago, just pay for it yourself, you cheapskate! Is there anything this grub won’t make us pay for? If you went out to dinner with Trump, he’d order everything on the menu then say I forgot my wallet, then ask you for 50 bucks, then put it into his wallet in front of you.” Jimmy Kimmel And on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host reacted to a new report finding that consumer confidence is now lower than it was during the pandemic. “Remember the good old days, when we thought our parents were going to die of a highly contagious disease?” he joked. “But don’t worry, the president says our nation is doing really well.” In a post on Truth Social, Trump claimed the US was doing “better than ever before, but the Public just doesn’t know how well we’re doing. The Fake News Media refuses to disseminate our Record Setting Numbers, so I’m doing the best I can to do it myself!” “No way he came up with ‘disseminate’ on his own,” Kimmel quipped. “He thinks disseminate is how he got stuck with Don Jr.” “The president right now is working very hard to right the ship that definitely isn’t sinking,” Kimmel continued. “Trump held an event yesterday to triumphantly announce a $54bn investment in natural gas,” though he appeared to doze off during it. “Only Donald Trump would fall asleep during a press conference with the secretary of energy,” Kimmel quipped.

webTitle: US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains

fields.headline: US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains
fields.trailText: Final jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%
fields.bodyText: US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election. The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of just under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added. Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years. The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady since last year, when it hit 4.5% in November. US jobless claims also inched lower for the fourth week in a row, the labor department said on Thursday. But a closer look at the data also reveals how not all Americans are experiencing the same labor market. Unemployment among Black Americans grew an entire percentage point to 7%, double the rate of white Americans. Though job growth slumped over the summer – the labor market unexpectedly contracted in July and figures in June and May were revised sharply down from initial reports – 162,000 jobs were added in August, the highest since March. Job openings and the number of hires have also remained little changed in August, according to the recent data from the labor department, as the “slow-hire, slow-fire” job market continues. Data from private employers released by the payroll firm, ADP, earlier this week had painted a much rosier picture of the labor market. It found that private sector hiring accelerated last month for the first time since May, carried by growth in the healthcare, education and hospitality industries, and private employers added 90,000 new jobs. The labor market has remained largely strong this year even as the US-Israel war on Iran has upped inflation, especially energy prices. Last month, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years, citing higher prices. At the time, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, emphasized the strength of the US labor market, which “is basically running consistent with full employment”, but he noted that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”. Though the data still reflects an overall solid jobs market, the September release cools expectations for the US Federal Reserve to increase rates again in its final meeting before the 3 November midterms. Most central bank officials penciled in at least one more rate hike before the year’s end, which is now more likely to come at the Fed’s December conference. But higher prices continue to be the biggest economic pain point for Americans. Mortgage rates accelerated to their highest level in three years on Thursday from 7% to 7.28%, the largest weekly jump since 2022. The 10-year treasury yield, which underpins mortgages and other loans, also reached a 24-year high as the recent global bond sell-off continued. Meanwhile, higher oil prices have cost Americans an estimated $936 per household.

webTitle: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now

fields.headline: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
fields.trailText: As they had in the past, San Ygnacio residents banded together to stop a development threatening their town
fields.bodyText: This story was co-published and supported by the journalism non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project. Joel Ruiz pointed his cane toward a long piece of metal lying in the dirt. Unwanted construction crews had left it behind on his riverfront property where he has lived and run a small fishing business for decades in San Ygnacio, Texas. At 90, Ruiz still tends the land. But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico. For months, Ruiz and a handful of other San Ygnacio residents have been trying to halt the construction of a federal border wall in their Mexican American town of roughly 400 people. They’ve blocked bulldozers, been arrested, unearthed 75-year-old land records and filed lawsuits challenging the federal government’s authority to build here. Even though residents say nearly all the riverfront land in the county is privately owned, the government is building on it anyway, claiming a decades-old right. While they have stopped construction on the disputed land for now – a verbal concession, not a court order – the reprieve is precarious: the lawsuits are unresolved, the federal money set aside for construction remains in place and residents know the crews could be back. But they are drawing on the memory of a town that rose up against the government once before. “This little spot is all we have,” said Elsa Hull, who owns property downriver with her two daughters. “But [residents] fought the federal government before and won – and we can do it again.” ‘Life or death for us’ Founded along the Rio Grande in 1830, San Ygnacio grew from a cluster of ranches into a small border town. Today, its plaza is still lined with homes made of sandstone quarried from the riverbank. The town sits in Zapata county, where roughly 38% of residents live below the poverty line and the median household income is about $39,000. Many work in healthcare, schools, food service and ranching. The border patrol is a major regional employer: its sector in Laredo employs about 3,025 people. The construction is part of the Trump administration’s renewed border-wall push – a roughly $46.5bn expansion funded by what is known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. San Ygnacio is located in one of the stretches where that money is now hitting the ground – and it’s going up as the number of border apprehensions is dropping drastically. Ruiz said he rarely sees anyone crossing this stretch of river any more. The Rio Grande is also San Ygnacio’s sole source of drinking water, and the wall is being built in its floodplain. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waived 30 federal laws – among them the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, eliminating the environmental review that would normally accompany a project of this scale. (The DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.) To fill that gap, the Laredo-based Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) commissioned its own. The assessment warned that the wall and buoy system along and in the Rio Grande would worsen flooding – and, in places, fail outright. “This is life or death for us,” said Tricia Cortez, the center’s executive director. A breach of the wall system, she warned, would be sudden and catastrophic – homes destroyed, lives endangered. “The wall will straitjacket the river, forcing flood waters to rise and move faster.” Construction in San Ygnacio had begun without notice. Residents watched what they called a “man camp” rise at its edge and sensed something was coming. At a June community meeting to discuss other business, word began spreading through the back of the room: contractors were clearing land along the riverbank. Several residents hurried down and confronted the equipment operators, telling them they were on private property. Hull spent 25 years as an environmental investigator for the Texas commission on environmental quality. She recalled how she would watch deer, bobcats, coyotes and sunsets over the river from a bench beneath a tree on the bluff. Border construction has since knocked the tree down and smashed the bench. “Every part of my life is intertwined with the Rio Grande,” Hull said. “To me this river is sacred.” When contractors arrived near Ruiz’s home and RV park in June, he invited Hull and her friend to see the damage done. Crews had razed trees and severed an irrigation line. Before leaving for an appointment, Ruiz signed a paper authorizing Hull and her friend to stay and watch the property. Two contractor trucks slipped through the gate. Hull said one worker repeatedly flashed a card marked “CBP” – presumably Customs and Border Protection. Then she noticed Southwest Valley Constructors identification on his vest. “You’re not CBP,” Hull recalled telling him. When another truck approached, Hull drove her car across the entrance. More trucks arrived, followed by sheriff’s deputies, state troopers and border patrol agents. “We were just surrounded by all these men,” Hull said. Hull pulled up the county appraisal map and argued the crews were on Ruiz’s property. A deputy insisted the land was federal. Finally, Hull put her water bottle on the hood of her car and sat down. “Fuck it,” she said. “Arrest me.” They did. On 14 August, Hull returned, carrying a flag that read “Keep Our River Free” on one side and “Walls and Buoys Kill” on the other. When a sheriff’s deputy called to her from across a fence, she thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she was handcuffed and arrested again. A win from the past San Ygnacio had fought the federal government for this land once before – and won. When government contractors insisted the land was federal, Frank “Chip” Briscoe, an architectural conservator, started digging through county records. The trail led back to the early 1950s, when the government built the Falcon dam. Its reservoir submerged historic ranch communities and Indigenous sites along the river, and San Ygnacio was scheduled to be condemned and cleared for the reservoir, too. But residents refused to accept it. In 1951, more than 200 people signed a petition, organized by local veterans and civic leaders, opposing the measure. It worked: the government carved San Ygnacio out of the condemnation, the one stretch along the river bend spared from the reservoir. Seventy years later, the town is invoking that same exclusion again. Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda searched subsequent property records and still found no evidence that the federal government had later acquired the excluded land. The documents gave De Anda something concrete to act on. In mid-June, he met with the US army corps of engineers on Ruiz’s behalf, arguing the crews had no legal grounds to build on the disputed property. When construction continued, De Anda sent a warning letter and filed two lawsuits against the federal government, alleging it took private property in violation of the fifth amendment. Two more landowners are preparing to sue, and De Anda plans to sue the contractor, Southwest Valley Constructors, in state court. Landowners filed criminal trespass complaints, while about a dozen residents pressed local officials to intervene. About a month later, according to De Anda, the county attorney arranged a meeting with contractors and federal officials. “They agreed to stop,” he said, and the crews pulled back – for now. For De Anda, stopping construction is only part of the plan. “Our strategy is to affect the national consciousness,” he said. The rest is a matter of time. Every day they hold the line – with their bodies, their deeds, their lawsuits – buys more of it. They are looking toward the midterms, hoping a change in Congress could give them another opening. They are betting they can outlast it. At San Ygnacio’s Grito de Septiembre festival, enlarged copies of the 1951 petition and its signature pages were displayed in the plaza. Residents gathered around them, searching for the names of their ancestors. Back on Ruiz’s land, people have stopped coming to fish for white bass and alligator gar; when construction began, it blocked his boat ramp access. The small fishing business he ran here is now, in his words, “kaput”. Still, Ruiz keeps coming to the river. In 1973, he helped establish a bird sanctuary beside his property. “My baby,” he called it. “I built it.” When asked whether his daily walks down to the river had become a way of watching for the crews to return – their equipment still sitting idle on the land – he shook his head. He was here “just to be here”, he said.

webTitle: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped

fields.headline: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped
fields.trailText: These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
fields.bodyText: A turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority. Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration. These charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought. Polling shows there has been a nationwide shift towards the Democrats in the run-up to the midterms, even in states Republicans have dominated for decades. Many recent surveys of the generic ballot, a key indicator of voters’ intent in congressional elections, give the Democrats an edge ranging from the high single digits to the low double digits. The events of this year – notably the Iran war and its impact on inflation – have undoubtedly changed the race, and much of the advantage seems to have swung towards the Democrats. Across all key races, Democratic candidates have been campaigning on affordability, at a time when the Trump administration’s actions in the Middle East have pushed up prices, particularly for gasoline and diesel. It is a reflection of just how concerned US voters are about the economy, rating it as the most important issue in surveys, far ahead of immigration, healthcare or civil rights. Meanwhile, Trump’s personal ratings have also fallen, with Reuters/Ipsos finding only 32% of US adults now approve of his job performance. That is worse than his previous low of 34%, recorded by Gallup at the end of his first term in 2021 after the January 6 attack on the US Capitol. The 2026 midterms may be another brutal reckoning for the US president – the question is whether punishment from voters will lead him to change course.

webTitle: Christa Pike left in ‘critical condition’ as Tennessee halts all executions | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Christa Pike in ‘critical condition’ as Tennessee halts all executions
fields.trailText: Failed attempt to execute 50-year-old prompts review of state’s execution practices amid distressing witness accounts
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Tennessee’s governor has suspended executions as Christa Pike’s lawyer says the state’s failed lethal injection execution attempt has left her in a critical condition. Bill Lee, the Republican state governor, has suspended all executions in the state until at least the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry. Leading voices on the death penalty in the US have told the Guardian that the failed execution was such a violation of the constitutional prohibition on “cruel and unusual punishment” that all judicial killings should be halted nationwide. What have Pike’s lawyers said about her condition? Randy Spivey, one of her attorneys, said: “We don’t have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment, but we do know that she is alive right now and receiving life-saving medical care. She is in a critical condition.” What did witnesses say took place during the execution attempt? Catherine Sweeney, a reporter at the Nashville Public Radio WPLN, said: “They went through two rounds, and she was still breathing at the end. She was very ragged. She lifted her head up and was looking around. At one point, she said … there was a spot that was burning and hurting, and asked if that was normal. None of it was normal.” What was Pike convicted of? She was convicted of the brutal 1995 killing of Colleen Slemmer, alongside her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp. Lee said he had not yet spoken to Slemmer’s family after the failed execution. Family of Renee Good sues administration officials and the ICE agent who shot her The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration on Thursday. In the lawsuits, Good’s partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers. Why has the DNC issued a lawsuit against the administration? The Trump administration broke the law when it pushed through a last-minute change to the form overseas citizens use to register and request absentee ballots, the Democratic National Committee (DNC) said in a lawsuit filed on Thursday. “Trump and Republicans are so desperate to hang on to power that they are trying to eliminate the way some American citizens abroad register to vote and request mail ballots,” said Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC. Which states are leading the resistance to the Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rules? Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The New York attorney general, Letitia James, said the federal government was showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations would pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution. Hegseth puts the future of warfare in the hands of major Maga donors By installing the tech billionaires Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to advisory roles in a Pentagon project about the future of warfare, the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has given extraordinary influence to two of Maga’s most significant campaign donors – and both men own companies that benefit from federal defense contracting. Luckey, 34, whose company is backed by Joshua Kushner’s equity fund, has acquired manufacturers of underwater drones, unmanned aerial vehicles, and space technology, and has already been voluble about his philosophy on warfare, saying he thought warfare in the second half of this century would involve “subterranean” conflict, with vehicles that can “move through the crust of the Earth the same way that submarines move through the water”. What have been the latest developments with US forces in the Middle East? The US military is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, as Donald Trump warned new strikes against Iran could be on the horizon. Given the personnel already in place in the Middle East, the move would bring the US naval presence to an unusually high number of more than 20,000 sailors and Marines as well as hundreds of aircraft. Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University. “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.” In other news … Google has rolled out a new Gemini AI model – but has restricted access over safety concerns. California’s attorney general, meanwhile, has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI over reports of rogue agents’ hacking. SpaceX launched a crew to the ISS successfully, with Jessica Watkins, the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit, making her second trip to the space station. Lawmakers have called for action on what they say are “plainly illegal” taxpayer-funded ads to promote Donald Trump in the run-up to the midterms. The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defense motion. Kanye West’s sold-out Russia concerts have been cancelled, organisers have confirmed. Russia’s foreign ministry had called the planned shows unacceptable due to the rapper’s “glorification” of Adolf Hitler. Stat of the day: Lyft agrees to pay California $272.5m in largest-ever wage theft settlement Lyft agreed to pay the state of California $272.5m to ⁠settle claims that it stole drivers’ wages by mislabeling them as independent contractors rather than employees. Culture pick: The 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked! From tropical disasters and doomed sci-fi epics to bribing Orson Welles and fending off a puma, Ryan Gilbey rates cinema’s most revealing glimpses behind the scenes. Don’t miss this: I’m allergic to the cold California’s Shauna Castaner recounts her extraordinary experience of gradually coming to realise that her condition was getting so severe she has to a keep a close watch on her body temperature and can’t eat chilled foods. … or this: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring Erasure were regulars on the Billboard chart in the 1980s and 90s with hits like Chains of Love, A Little Respect and Always. They return with their 20th – TWENTIETH! – studio album. Tim Jonze speaks to the iconic British synthpop duo. Climate check: Think more rain means more river water? Not necessarily More rain and snow equals more water in rivers, right? Not necessarily. A new study shows that, despite receiving more rainfall than they used to, river water levels are falling because of changes in climate. Last Thing: Bear treats itself to baked goods at Colorado farmers’ market One animal in Aspen, Colorado, seemed to decide to make a late bid to win Fat Bear Week, as it rocked up to a farmers’ market and started devouring fresh bread and pastries at one of the stalls. webTitle: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgages

fields.headline: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgages
fields.trailText: The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some headway
fields.bodyText: When Maga media blowhard Clay Travis offered $2m to Colin Kaepernick last week to appear on the daily talkshow he hosts with former CIA analyst Buck Sexton, it represented the culmination of a years-long obsession on the right with the onetime NFL star. In Travis’s telling of history, Kaepernick taking a knee during the 2016 NFL season was the event that catalyzed professional sports into the era of “woke” excess from which, he claims, it has been struggling to recover ever since. But more than simply confirming the right’s longstanding villainization of Kaepernick, Travis’s offer was also a smarmy bid for publicity for his new media venture, Sport & State. Sport & State, which launched in August, is Travis’s bid to get back to his roots as a media mogul who sold the wildly popular Outkick to Fox Sports for a rumored $100m, and reclaim some of the cultural territory lost to fellow sports bros and Magagitators like Pat McAfee, Joe Rogan, Tucker Carlson and Ben Shapiro. But if there’s one thing Sport & State won’t be doing, it’s engaging with anyone beyond the Magaverse. There has been no response from Kaepernick since Travis made his “offer” of $2m to charity in exchange for an interview, which suggests he understands that it was extended more in a spirit of trolling buffoonery than sincerity. No one associated with the left or progressive politics ever appears on Travis’s shows, for the simple reason that they are designed purely for the right to talk to itself. (Some would say the same could be said of the left, although the disregard for dissenting perspectives in the Magasphere seems way more extreme.) More than it heralds a renewal of Travis’s career or an injection of fresh energy into the Trumpist mediasphere, Sport & State is a case study in the stagnation that has taken hold on the right as Donald Trump stares down the barrel of defeat in November’s midterm elections. Having spent the better part of the past two months listening to the Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show (which runs from noon to 3pm ET every weekday) and the Clay Travis Show (3-4pm), I can say with confidence that there are, in essence, only 11 topics a given day’s programming on Sport & State will cover: college football gambling picks; Trumpworld figures who are friends with Travis and Sexton; the wonderful job that these figures are doing in power (sometimes mixed with the preceding theme: “Our friend Kash, who is truly our friend, Clay and I are both buddies with him, he’s a good man,” Sexton affirmed on a recent episode); the low levels of testosterone apparently common among white males who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 (“white dudes for Kamala” is perhaps the gravest slur on the Clay Travis Show); trans women in professional sport (I haven’t calculated this precisely but at a guess I’d say this accounts for 20% to 50% of the discussion on any show that Travis hosts, even as the number of actual trans women competing in professional American sports remains exactly zero and there are probably fewer than 10 trans athletes in total in college sports); crime in America’s cities (in recent weeks the fixation has been Lindsay Clancy, but it’s liable to switch at any moment to Iryna Zarutska, Luigi Mangione, Charlie Kirk, Iryna Zarutska, or whatever murder happens to have taken place on that particular day in New York City); the problem with women (in summary: they are women); the fact that Travis and Sexton are both family men with wives and children; the fact that Travis has a law degree from Vanderbilt University; the fact that Travis studied law at Vanderbilt after he was rejected by Stanford (“I wanted to go to Stanford Law School, they didn’t want me, I went to Vanderbilt instead – I’ve now made a $10m donation to Vanderbilt Law School”); and the fact that Travis appeared on Fox News last night and will appear on Fox News again later today. Sprinkled throughout all of this are plugs for Hard Rock Bet (“Bet $5, get $100 in bonus bets”), which is the official gambling partner of Sport & State and holds equity in Travis’s upstart media concern, and companies such as Perfect 10 Mortgage, Crockett Coffee, XX-XY Athletics and Clay Travis Law, all of which – it should come as no surprise – Travis either outright owns or holds a stake in. The recursiveness and self-referentiality of the advertising and content on Sport & State are all part of the site’s commercial strategy, according to Travis’s lengthy mission statement. The onshoring of all the advertising will, Travis claims, insulate his new venture from the vagaries of media’s traditional dependence on subscriptions and external advertisers. Gambling is the key revenue driver: Outkick became an affiliate of FanDuel after sports betting was legalized in 2018 and eventually made $350 for every new gambling account it helped set up, netting $2m in affiliate betting revenue on Super Bowl Sunday in 2021 alone, and Sport & State is set up to reap similar rewards through its partnership with Hard Rock Bet. But Travis’s expectation is that his home loan business, say, will also prosper as viewers stay online to hear his views on Ole Miss v LSU, Lane Kiffin or the apparent attempted hijacking of the Israel-bound passenger jet and what it means for the future of DEI in America. Inadvertently, perhaps, Travis’s sidequest companies offer a sense of what Sport & State’s ideal audience member looks like: a patriotic American male with a habit of deploying the phrase “perfect 10” unironically whose life revolves around mortgages, coffee, litigation, gambling and moaning about trans women. On the Crockett Coffee blog, recent posts include “American Coffee Origins and Brewing Techniques”, “Discovering American Coffee’s Unique Flavors”, and “The Americano: A Complete History” (do I detect a theme here?); Travis sips throughout the day on Sport & State from a black spillproof coffee container, emphasizing his own commitment to the cause of caffeine and country. If there’s a persistent “Spider-Men pointing at each other” quality to the advertising on Sport & State, that extends to the content as well. Travis’s big idea is that in the age of AI and commodified writing, it’s better to go deep than big, that depth of audience commitment matters more than the old traffic era’s scale-focused contest for clicks. There may be some wisdom in the strategy, but that approach – drumming down and appeasing an already loyal base – seems to have become the media-obsessed Trump White House’s guiding political strategy too, a choice that risks self-sabotage as the midterms loom. Travis’s theory of media is second-term Trump’s theory of power: instead of growing the audience, the electorate, the constituency, the sole purpose of having attention is to give those listening more of the same. Discussion on Sport & State this week included a summary of Travis and Sexton’s Monday meeting with Trump in the Oval Office. Their main point was to emphasize that “President Trump says he loves the show, says we’re doing a great job” and that various Trumpworld figures greeted them during their half-hour in front of the Resolute Desk. “We saw Karoline Leavitt, our very good friend”; “We also saw Susie Wiles – she said she is cancer-free now”; “We got a little quick high-five from Stephen Miller”. Over a chyron announcing THE VOICE OF SEAN HANNITY, the longtime Fox News host then called in to discuss: sports betting (what else?); the border collie he’s about to take delivery of at the conclusion of nine months of dog training (if this is what it takes to survive domestic cohabitation with Hannity as an animal, imagine how things must be for the humans in his house); Gavin Newsom and Kathy Hochul as the highest-taxing, and therefore worst, governors in America; and potential Democratic candidates for 2028 (Hannity thinks AOC will be the nominee, Travis thinks it will be Kamala Harris; they agreed to bet on the outcome, with the loser to buy the winner a steak dinner in a demonstration of red-blooded American masculinity). The segment concluded with Hannity, Sexton and Travis all saying “we had an awesome time” after five minutes of meandering conversation about nothing, and the welcome announcement that Travis would be on Hannity’s show on Fox the following day for more of the same. On the right, the Spider-Men are always pointing at each other, and they’re all the audience each other needs. Watching Sport & State’s live programming and reading its endless churn of tiresome posts about how sports and the world suck now because of Joe Biden and woke, it’s difficult to figure out what, exactly, the appeal of Travis as a right-wing media personality is. Rogan has the vague charisma of a lifelong stoner; McAfee has that dog in him, a kind of American mongrel who forever puts himself next to a gas pump or under the chassis of a hoisted car; Carlson has a habit of Mozart-laughing at his own jokes, which is at the very least engagingly bizarre; Shapiro … well, Shapiro doesn’t have much going for him, but he does talk quickly. Travis, by contrast, has neither a sense of personal style nor any real sense of humor; he’s a boring dad who drones on endlessly about mortgages and failed sports bets and his law degree. He also frequently looks exhausted on air, as does Sexton; together they form perhaps the puffiest-looking duo in American media. Who knows? Perhaps a pair of hungover-looking permadads sipping mournfully from their coffee canisters while they bemoan the latest poll numbers out of Ohio is exactly the new groove the right needs to salvage a listing presidency. But it seems unlikely. Travis claims he’s working “20 hours a day” to produce material for Sport & State, and perhaps it really does take that long to package up clips from the previous 24 hours’ appearances on the Sean Hannity Show and Jesse Watters Primetime and Titans on Tomorrow with Ben Shapiro, brew the Crockett Coffee and get it into the spillproof containers, go on air, play the clips, then restate their substance using different words 500 times in a row. But if this is the right’s idea of a bold new intervention in sports and media, it’s hard not to feel that as a cultural force, the Magaverse is now well and truly running on fumes.

webTitle: Trump doesn’t rule out sending ICE to polling sites; US supreme court to review policy to detain immigrants challenging deportation – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump doesn’t rule out sending ICE to polling sites; US supreme court to review policy to detain immigrants challenging deportation – as it happened
fields.trailText: Justices will consider whether immigrants have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: In remarks to supporters in Texas and Oklahoma, Donald Trump lied that James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate who is challenging Republican Ken Paxton, is a vegan, a word he mispronounced “vaygan”. The White House refused to let CNN travel with Trump, but the president did stop to take questions from reporters for partidan rightwing outlets who were permitted to fly with him on Air Force. Lawyers for Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin Democrat running for Congress, have threatened to sue Republican congressman Derrick Van Orden for posting AI-generated deepfake videos of her on social media. Lawyers for Rebecca Cooke, a Wisconsin Democrat running for Congress, have threatened to sue Republican congressman Derrick Van Orden for posting AI-generated deepfake videos of her on social media. The letter pointed to one recent clip posted by Van Orden on X, apparently created with Grok, which showed an AI version of Cooke apparently admitting to corruption. A second deepfake created a fictional version of Cooke shouting at voters and calling them “peasants”. “I am the Anointed One. You will comply and you will vote for me,” the fake version of the candidate says. “That is an order from your DC masters.” “Apparently unable to run a campaign based on the issues, you have made AI deepfakes a centerpiece of your attacks on Ms. Cooke, posting myriad such videos,” the letter to Van Orden reads. It goes on: Take, for example, the video posted to your X account on August 4, 2026. It purports to show Ms. Cooke speaking “on the campaign trail” in Eau Claire with former President Biden seated behind her. The video attributes to Ms. Cooke the statement that she seeks “to take advantage of as much corruption as possible and give every illegal alien free healthcare.” The video is pure fiction. The events depicted did not occur. Ms. Cooke never made the statements attributed to her. She does not support, and has never supported, the positions ascribed to her in this deepfake. You are airing this false content to attempt to fool the voters of Wisconsin into believing she said something she did not to harm her reputation for your own political gain. Donald Trump’s remarks to supporters in Oklahoma on Thursday night repeated much of what he’s said at previous rallies, including a few hours ago in Texas. The president did, however, add an aside about his favorite shows on two partisan conservative networks, Fox News and Newsmax, which perhaps helps to explain how genuinely baffled he appears to be at his plunging poll numbers. “You know, I watch some of the shows – like Sean Hannity, Jesse, Laura,” Trump said, referring to the whole Fox primetime lineup of opinion hosts who openly support him: Sean Hannity, Jesse Watters and Laura Ingraham. He then added three Newsmax hosts: “Greg Kelly, Rob, I mean… take a look at Finnerty. You take a look at Schmitt.” “There are a lot of great shows,” the president said before adding: “We have more support than you think.” “We have such great support,” Trump said, reflecting his impression that praise from cable news hosts is the true barometer of popularity. “But I wish we could have more, I wish we could have more the media support.” Later in the speech, as if to illustrate that he does, indeed, live inside a rightwing media bubble, Trump told the crowd about how happy he was to see three men waiting to enter the arena praising him on television. The president then had his aides play the clip for the crowd, before calling the men to the stage. As Trump watched the clip along with the crowd, he did not appear to react to the fact that the interview included a mention of the fact that Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, had been caught on audio recently suggesting that Trump’s support for him was a drag on his campaign. Later in the speech, Trump told the crowd more about his television viewing habits. “A person was on the other night, a beautiful woman defending me, and she was defending me against the radical left lunatics,” Trump said. “And she said, you know, ‘he did this, he did that, he did that, that, that, that’. And then she said … ‘I was writing the stuff last night for the show, and I ran out of paper’ … it was sort of cool.” Donald Trump has begun speaking to supporters at a rally in Oklahoma, near the state’s border with Texas. He began his remarks by repeating the same lie about Democrat James Talarico he told in Texas earlier: that the Senate candidate is a vegan who only pretends to eat meat. As he did in Texas, Trump repeatedly mispronounced vegan, as “vaygan”. “You know, he’s a vaygan in Texas,” Trump said. “But now he’s trying to pretend he’s not a vaygan.” In fact, Talarico is not a vegan and has frequently been photographed eating meat. “I said it just before, I hate to bore you if you’ve heard it,” the president said, aware that he was repeating himself. “So he goes out and he goes to barbecues and he has meat. And every time he goes up, he says, ‘excuse me just for a moment’. He goes to the back of the tent and he throws up all of it.” Trump told this same imaginary tale at the midterm Republican convention in Dallas last month, despite the fact that there is no evidence that Talarico ever said or did anything like this. On Thursday evening, the Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin primed a crowd of Oklahoma supporters awaiting Donald Trump with a conspiracy theory: Democrats are plotting a communist takeover of the nation. “In order for them to take us to a socialist country and move us right into a communist country, they have to create chaos… they’ve got to change the demographics,” Mullin said, referring to the presence of undocumented immigrants. “They’ve got to usher in chaos. And then they’ll come out and say ‘Hey look this government doesn’t work.
